title: kalau — if, when
pattern: Kalau A, B · B kalau A · Kalau saya, …
explanation: kalau sets a condition: Kalau ada waktu, main ke rumah, ya. — If you've got time, come over. The kalau part usually comes first, with a comma, but it can also follow: Telepon saya kalau ada masalah. Because verbs don't show tense, kalau also covers when for things that haven't happened yet: Kalau sudah sampai, kabari saya. Before a person or thing it means as for: Kalau saya, nasi goreng saja. And Kalau begitu (casual Kalau gitu) is the set phrase for in that case.
natural: The everyday if, polite or casual; in fast speech it sounds like kalo, though it's still written kalau. It's also a gentle way to suggest or bargain: Kalau seratus ribu, boleh?
stiff: jika and apabila are the written ifs of signs, forms and announcements; in a conversation they sound like a contract. For a one-off when in the past (when I was in Bali), use waktu, not kalau.

examples.indonesian: Kalau ada waktu, main ke rumah, ya.
examples.english: If you've got time, come over to my place.

gap.after: ada waktu, main ke rumah, ya.
gap.why: They may or may not have time: a condition takes kalau. Karena would mean you know they're free.

examples.indonesian: Kalau sudah sampai, kabari saya, ya.
examples.english: Let me know when you get there.

gap.why: Getting there hasn't happened yet, so when is kalau; waktu is for a time that's already past.

examples.english: As for me, just fried rice.

gap.why: Kalau before a person means as for: kalau saya, as for me.

examples.indonesian: Hari ini penuh? Kalau begitu, besok saja.
examples.english: Today's full? In that case, tomorrow, then.

gap.why: Kalau begitu is a set phrase: in that case.
